Proteins being sorted, packaged into vesicles and shipped out

knockouts.claim: Glycolysis keeps going — in creatine-kinase-deficient mouse muscle it actually speeds up and carries more of the energy flow — but quick ATP bursts are lost.
Glycolysis in the cytosol carries on as normal. What breaks is the muscle cell's contraction machinery, because the thin filaments of the sarcomere cannot form properly.
Glucose keeps crossing the membrane normally, because GLUT transporters do that job. What stops is the sodium rush that lets the neuron fire an electrical signal.
Glucose still crosses the membrane, since that needs transporters, not SNAREs. What fails is fusing neurotransmitter-filled vesicles with the membrane, so the neuron cannot release its message.
The Golgi keeps sorting and packaging the beta cell's other proteins. What is missing is insulin itself, so no insulin-filled granules are made or released.
In a beta or liver cell, glucose gets its first phosphate tag much more slowly, so glycolysis starts sluggishly and the cell senses sugar poorly.
The liver cell's Golgi keeps packaging and shipping its other proteins. Albumin simply isn't there to pack, so none leaves the cell.
The ER keeps building and sending on proteins as usual. What the cell loses is the ER's ability to chemically alter many drugs and vitamin D.
Glycolysis still runs — it is the red blood cell's only ATP source. What the cell loses is working hemoglobin, so it cannot carry oxygen.
In a red blood cell GLUT1 is the only glucose door, so glucose essentially stops entering; other cells use GLUT2, GLUT3 or GLUT4 instead.
ATP synthase cannot assemble properly, so the mitochondrion makes much less ATP. The cell leans on glycolysis instead, and lactic acid builds up.
The nucleus keeps making RNA copies of genes. What changes is which ones: genes for building mitochondria are switched on much less strongly.
Glycolysis carries on unchanged; myoglobin stores oxygen rather than breaking down sugar. Myoglobin-free mouse muscle still performed normally in standard tests.
No other enzyme in the cell does GAPDH's step, so glycolysis halts there; the backup gene GAPDHS works only in sperm.
